segments.text: Watching a chatbot like ChatGPT or Claude respond to a complex request feels seamless.
You type a prompt, and a coherent essay begins to materialize on the screen, word by word,
in real time.
Despite that fluid interface, there is no conscious mind driving the response.
These systems operate on a foundation of mathematical logic, specifically a branch of mathematics
known as probability, the study of how likely something is to happen.
Every time an artificial intelligence generates a response, it is simply calculating the probability
of which word should appear next.
To understand how these modern tools operate, we actually have to look backward to the historical
foundations of that math.
The modern rules of probability were born in 1654, when two French mathematicians, Blaise
Pascal and Pierre de Fermat, traded letters trying to solve a problem about gambling odds.
Their work gave us a foundational rule for calculating odds when every possible outcome
is equally likely.
This graphic shows the standard probability formula.
It's calculated by taking the ways to get a specific result and dividing it by the
total possible outcomes.
The top number represents the exact scenario you are looking for, and the bottom number
accounts for every single thing that could possibly happen.
This simple faction, just counting up the possibilities, is the building block for all predictive
math.
Let's apply that formula to a physical scenario.
Say you toss two standard coins, and you want to know the chances that both will land
on heads.
This infographic shows four distinct, equally likely outcomes for tossing two coins.
Looking across the board, only one option gives us double heads.
Plugging those numbers into our baseline formula, 1 divided by 4 gives us a 25% probability,
that 25% represents our mathematical reality before we have any outside evidence.
It is a completely blind guess.
Now let's introduce a twist.
You toss the two coins again, but this time someone peeks at the first coin that lands
and tells you definitively that it's heads.
This introduces what mathematicians call conditional probability.
When new evidence arrives, we are forced to update our math.
Based on this new information, which outcomes are no longer possible?
Since the first coin is heads, we cross off the outcomes starting with tails.
Recounting, we have one way to get double heads out of two remaining outcomes, changing
our probability to 50%.
The physical coins themselves didn't change when someone saw the result.
What changed was our knowledge.
This added context alone shifted the odds from 25 to 50%.
This exact concept of conditional probability is what drives the AI apps we use every day.
When you type a prompt into a chatbot, your text functions like the peeked coin.
It's the evidence the system needs to start its calculation.
Let's say you type a prompt, asking the AI, what should I name my new dog?
The words in your question, and any words the AI has already started typing in response,
act as constraints that eliminate impossible or unlikely next words.
Just as the knowledge of that first coin ruled out tails, conversational context rules out
unrelated dictionary words, narrowing the AI's focus to a highly probable set of choices.
This graphic shows the AI's mathematical reality mid-sentence, as it replies,
you could name him, and calculates the blank.
The AI evaluates top probabilities for the next word, spot at 22%, max at 17, and buddy
at 14.
The remaining 47% is distributed across thousands of other words.
Once the AI selects a word, like spot, that choice instantly becomes a new piece of data,
altering the conditional probability for whatever word must come after it.
The process repeats continuously.
AI isn't conjuring thoughts from thin air.
It builds answers through probabilistic tabulations, one prediction at a time.
